content: Kigelia is a genus of flowering plants belonging to the family Bignoniaceae. This genus contains only one species, Kigelia africana, which is distributed across tropical Africa, ranging from Eritrea and Chad in the north to northern South Africa in the south, and extending westward to Senegal and Namibia. The genus name Kigelia is derived from the Mozambican Bantu term kigeli-keia. Its common name, Sausage Tree, refers to the elongated, sausage-shaped fruit it produces. In Afrikaans, it is called Worsboom, which also translates to Sausage Tree, while its Arabic name means the father of kit bags (Roodt, 1992). The tree can grow up to 20 meters in height. Its bark is initially smooth and gray but peels as the tree ages. On a branch with a diameter of 15 cm, the bark can be as thick as 6 mm (Roodt, 1992). The wood is pale brown or yellowish, undifferentiated, and resistant to cracking (Roodt, 1992). Kigelia africana is evergreen in regions with year-round rainfall but becomes deciduous in areas with prolonged dry seasons. The leaves are arranged oppositely or in whorls of three, measuring 30–50 cm in length. They are pinnate, with six to ten oval leaflets that can grow up to 20 cm long and 6 cm wide. The terminal leaflet may or may not be present. The flowers, and later the fruit, hang from the branches on long, flexible stems that can reach lengths of 2–6 meters. The flowers are produced in panicles and are bell-shaped, resembling those of the African tulip tree but darker and waxier. They are orange to reddish or purplish-green in color and approximately 10 cm wide. Unlike the fruit, the individual flowers are oriented horizontally rather than hanging downward. Certain bird species are attracted to these flowers, and the sturdy stems provide ideal perches. The flowers emit a strong scent, particularly at night, suggesting that they rely on bats for pollination. Bats visit the flowers to feed on pollen and nectar. The fruit is a woody berry that measures 30–100 cm in length and up to 18 cm in width, weighing between 5–10 kg. It hangs from long, rope-like peduncles. The fruit pulp is fibrous and contains numerous seeds. Various mammals, including baboons, bushpigs, savannah elephants, giraffes, hippopotami, monkeys, and porcupines, consume the fruit. The seeds are dispersed through their dung. Additionally, the seeds are eaten by brown parrots and brown-headed parrots, while the foliage is consumed by elephants and greater kudu (Joffe, 2003; del Hoyo et al., 1997). In Australia, introduced specimens of Kigelia africana are popular among cockatoos in parks. Cultivation and Uses In African herbal medicine, the fruit of Kigelia africana is believed to treat a wide range of ailments, including rheumatism, snakebites, syphilis, and even supernatural afflictions or tornadoes (Watkins, 1975). An alcoholic beverage similar to beer is also made from the fruit. However, the fresh fruit is toxic and has strong purgative properties. To make it safe for consumption, the fruit is prepared by drying, roasting, or fermentation (Joffe, 2003; McBurney, 2004). In Botswana, the timber is used to craft makoros (traditional dugout canoes), yokes, and oars (Roodt, 1992). The tree is widely cultivated as an ornamental species in tropical regions due to its striking flowers and unusual fruit. However, care must be taken when selecting planting sites, as the falling fruit can cause serious injuries to people and damage vehicles parked beneath the trees. Kigelia is also used in various skincare products, with one notable example being African Earthworks Kigelia. These products are designed to mitigate the damage caused by the harsh African sun. Synonymy Some synonyms for Kigelia africana are still recognized by a few horticulturists as distinct species. However, botanical studies confirm that the genus contains only one species (Joffe, 2003; GRIN). Synonyms include: Bignonia africana Lam. (basionym) Tecoma africana (Lam.) Don Crescentia pinnata Jacq. Kigelia pinnata (Jacq.) DC. Kigelia aethiopica Decne.
